The supporting force on the load is vertical and the displacement is horizontal, so the work done is zero. A is false and R is true.
I: W = −∫μ0 mg(1 − x/L) dx from 0 to L = −μ0 mgL/2, not −μ0 mgL, so I is incorrect. II: W = F·d = 2(1) + 3(−2) + (−1)(3) = −7 J, so II is correct.
K = p²/2m. Doubling p (a 100% increase) makes K four times larger, so K increases by 300%.
dU/dx = x² - 4 = 0 gives x = ±2. d²U/dx² = 2x is positive at x = +2, so U is a minimum there and the equilibrium is stable.
K = p²/2m with equal p, so K is proportional to 1/m. K1:K2 = 4:1.
Minimum of U is stable (III). Maximum of U is unstable (IV). Constant U is neutral (I). dU/dx > 0 means F = -dU/dx < 0, so the force is along -x (II).

A is true: KE = mv²/2 cannot be negative. B is true: PE depends on the reference level. C is false: friction is non-conservative, so no PE exists for it. D is false: for equal p, the heavier body has less KE. E is true: tripling v gives 9 times the KE. Correct set is A, B, E.
The friction deceleration is a = μg = 3 m/s². So d = v²/(2a) = 36/6 = 6 m.
Loss of PE = 2×10×5 = 100 J. Gain in KE = ½×2×64 = 64 J. Work by friction = 64 − 100 = −36 J.
Fd = KE, so equal KE and equal force give equal distance: A is true. The work-energy theorem holds for all forces, so R is false.
I: d ∝ v², so doubling speed gives 4× distance, true. II: W = ∫x dx from 0 to 3 = 4.5 J, so ½v² = 4.5 and v = 3 m/s, true.
Constant power gives (1/2)mv^2 = Pt, so v ∝ t^(1/2) and s ∝ t^(3/2). Distance in 4t is 4^(3/2)s = 8s

By energy conservation, v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2*10*20) = 20 m/s.
Drop in height h = L(1 - cos60°) = 2.5*0.5 = 1.25 m. So v = sqrt(2*10*1.25) = 5 m/s.
Loss of potential energy = mgh = 100 J. Final kinetic energy = (1/2)(2)(64) = 64 J. Work done by friction = 64 - 100 = -36 J.
Assuming the body is released from rest at height H, total energy is mgH. KE at H/2 = mgH/2 (II). PE at H/4 = mgH/4 (I). KE at H/4 = mgH - mgH/4 = 3mgH/4 (III). Total mechanical energy = mgH (IV).

A is true: v = sqrt(2gh), independent of the path. B is false: speed does not depend on mass. C is true: friction does negative work equal to the change in mechanical energy. D is false: total energy of an isolated system is conserved. E is true: at h/2, KE = PE = mgh/2.
Work done by air resistance depends on the path taken and is always dissipative, so air resistance is non-conservative. Gravitational, electrostatic and ideal spring forces are conservative.
Friction f = μmg = 0.2×5×10 = 10 N. It always opposes motion, so it does negative work on both legs. Total path = 8 m, so W = -10×8 = -80 J.
A is true because kinetic friction is non-conservative, so no potential energy function exists for it. R is false because friction does negative, non-zero work around a closed path.
Statement I is incorrect: the correct relation is W_c = -ΔU = U_i - U_f. Statement II is incorrect: gravity is conservative, so its work between two fixed points is path-independent.
For a string, the tension at the top can fall to zero, so the minimum speed at the bottom is v = √(5gL) = √(5×10×2) = 10 m/s.
A rigid rod can push as well as pull, so the speed at the top can be zero. Energy conservation gives v = √(4gL) = √(4×10×0.4) = 4 m/s.

Assuming the bob is given the minimum speed √(5gL): tension at the bottom is 6mg. With the string horizontal, v² = 3gL and T = 3mg. Tension at the top is zero. Speed with the string horizontal is √(3gL). So A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

A is true: √(2gL) < √(3gL) < √(5gL), so the string slackens above the horizontal. B is true: √(gL) < √(2gL), so the bob oscillates below the horizontal. C is false: the 6mg difference holds for any speed while the string stays taut. D is true: a bead on a ring needs only √(4gR). E is false: tension is greatest at the lowest point, so the string breaks there. Correct set: A, B, D.
In a head-on elastic collision between equal masses, the bodies exchange velocities. So the first body stops and the second moves off with speed u.
Common velocity = (2×6)/6 = 2 m/s. Initial KE = ½×2×36 = 36 J. Final KE = ½×6×4 = 12 J. Loss = 36 − 12 = 24 J.

For an oblique elastic collision of equal masses with one at rest, the final velocities are perpendicular. The second ball moves at 60° to the original direction. So v1 = u cos30° = √3u/2 and v2 = u sin30° = u/2.
A is false: only the KE relative to the centre of mass is lost, and KE remains if total momentum is nonzero. R is a correct description of a perfectly inelastic collision.
v1 = (1−4)/5 × 10 = −6 m/s, so the ball rebounds at 6 m/s and I is false. v2 = 2×1/5 × 10 = 4 m/s, KE2 = ½×4×16 = 32 J out of 50 J = 64%, so II is true.
